messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 48
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Waiter/Waitress
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside

Vignette:
Linh Phạm is a 48-year-old Vietnamese-American woman, divorced, who works as a waitress at a mid-sized restaurant in a suburban strip mall. She was referred for psychological assessment following a brief conversation with her primary care physician, to whom she had gone complaining of fatigue and difficulty sleeping. When the physician asked a few careful questions, Linh began to cry in a way that surprised even her — quietly, and with what looked like shame.

Approximately fourteen months ago, a man began appearing at the restaurant where Linh works. At first she assumed he was simply a regular customer who had taken a liking to the food. He sat in her section each time, always ordered the same thing, and left generous tips with handwritten notes tucked beneath the receipt. Within a few weeks the notes had become personal — commenting on her hair, her laugh, the way she moved between tables. Then he began waiting for her in the parking lot after her shifts, stepping out from between cars as she walked to her vehicle. He knew her name, her schedule, and eventually her home address. Over the following three months he appeared outside her apartment building on multiple occasions, once pressing his face against the glass of the lobby door while she stood frozen in the hallway, unable to move toward the exit or back toward the elevator. She had come to believe, in those moments, that her body had simply stopped belonging to her — that it was a thing being watched and catalogued by someone else, and that she had no authority over it. A restraining order was eventually obtained, and the man relocated out of state following a criminal complaint. Legally, the threat was resolved. Psychologically, it was not.

In the months that followed, Linh found that the memory of his face at the lobby glass did not behave like an ordinary memory. It arrived without invitation — while she was folding napkins at the start of a shift, while she was rinsing a cup at her kitchen sink — and when it came, it brought with it a wave of physical sensation so complete that her hands would shake and her chest would tighten as though the event were still unfolding. What disturbed her most was that she could not seem to narrate what had happened to her in any coherent way. When her daughter asked what the man had done, Linh found herself unable to answer. The experience existed somewhere in her body and in flashes of image and sensation, but it resisted language. And stranger still, when she tried to recall it deliberately, it felt as though it had happened to someone else entirely — a woman she had read about, not herself.

At work, the consequences became concrete and cumulative. Linh began to dread tables occupied by men who sat alone and watched the room. When the restaurant was short-staffed and she was asked to cover a section she didn't know well, she would feel the familiar tightening begin — she had come to feel that unfamiliar spaces were spaces she could not read for danger, and so she avoided them when possible, trading sections with younger colleagues and absorbing their confusion with tight-lipped apologies. Any minor friction with a customer — a complaint about wait time, a returned dish — sent her into a state of acute distress she could not explain to her managers. She had stopped seeing the two friends she used to meet for coffee on Sunday mornings, finding reasons to cancel until the invitations stopped coming. She no longer glanced at herself in the bathroom mirror before her shifts. She had come to feel that attending to her own body in any deliberate way was something she could not bear.

At home, she lay awake listening for sounds at the door — the elevator, footsteps in the corridor, any creak that might mean someone was approaching. She described herself to her physician as feeling dead inside, and said it without drama, as a simple report. She used to be someone who laughed easily, she said. She used to care about things. She could no longer locate that person.

What finally brought her to the intake appointment was her daughter's wedding, scheduled for six months from now. Linh wanted to be present for it — truly present — and she was afraid, with a quiet and specific terror, that she no longer knew how.
